lectures.title: Building For Production & Understanding NextJS Caching

cues.en: So sharing meals works now,
but there actually is one problem with our application.
Everything works fine here during development when using
that development server,
but things will change once we move to production.
Now, to move from development to production, we should quit
that development server here
and then run another script in the terminal,
navigate it into our project folder still.
And that's the NPM Run build script.
This will build
and prepare our NextJS application for production.
It will essentially give us a project
that we could then deploy onto a server.
Now you can run that production server
and that optimized code by then running NPM start.
So first NPM run build, and then thereafter NPM start.
This will start a server,
but now not some development server,
but instead the production server,
which here is still served under the same address,
but now it's serving that optimized code and so on.
Now therefore you can revisit local host 3000
and you should, for example, still see your meals there,
but you'll now notice something strange
when you add a new meal.
For that, I'll again, going to enter some data
and I'll name my meal, tasty Bruschetta,
Very delicious.
Add my instructions like this
and pick the same image as always.
If I now click share meal, I'm redirected.
And this is now quicker, as I mentioned before.
That's great, it's quicker, better user experience,
but the meal is missing here.
I see the three meals I submitted before,
but this new meal is missing.
Keep in mind that I added a text of very delicious to it
and I don't see that text anywhere here.
And there's one other thing
that's pretty strange here on this site.
If I go back to the starting page for example, and I reload
and I then go to browse meals,
I'm there pretty much instantly.
If I'm on this page and I reload,
it also reloads pretty much instantly.
You might recall that before, this took five seconds
because I added this extra delay here in the meals.js file,
this delay.
Why is this missing here in production
and why is this meal we added missing?
Well, because as mentioned earlier in this section,
NextJS performs some pretty aggressive caching
and there is one extra step it performs
and goes through when preparing the app for production
that we didn't see when testing it
with the development server.
Because when you run this NPM run build command
to prepare the app for production, NextJS goes ahead
and actually generates, pre-renders all the pages
of your app that can be pre-generated,
so basically all non-dynamic pages.
So it, for example, pre-generated the meals page.
So this page.js file in the meals folder,
this page here, which outputs some meals,
it was pre-generated, so all that data was fetched
and rendered there during the build process.
And NextJS is doing that
because by pre-rendering all these pages,
it of course has those pages available right
from the start after being deployed.
And so the very first visitor of your website is able
to instantly see the finished page without having to wait
for anything to render,
which of course can be a great user experience.
And NextJS then caches those pre-rendered pages so
that it's able to serve them to all visitors.
But the downside of this approach, of course,
is that it never re-fetches the meals
because this code here never executes again.
Instead, it just uses those pre-generated pages.
And I can prove that we can simply console log,
fetching meals here in that meals component
that's being used by the meals page.
And if I do that and I then rebuild my project
by running NPM run build again, you will see
that it generates all those pages
and then once it's done, if I start that production server,
if I reload the meals page, I don't see fetching meals here.
I get some warning that we might want
to install some extra package when using
that image component, but we can ignore that here.
The main thing is
that we don't see this message being logged,
so that is not executing anymore
because those pages were pre-generated and cached.
But that's of course a problem if the data that's visible on
that page changes as is the case for me here.
Now you can see that latest meal I added earlier now
because I regenerated all the pages,
but if I would add another new meal here,
it would again be missing.
And that's of course
absolutely not the behavior we want here.
So how can we fix this problem
of NextJS caching too aggressively?
Well, we need to tell NextJS to throw away its cache
or parts of its cache whenever we add a new meal.
And of course, this is such a common requirement
that there's a built-in method for that,
a built-in function provided by NextJS,
a function which I wanna execute in my server action
right after saving a meal before I redirect.
And that function is called revalidatePath.
This function tells NextJS
to revalidate the cache
that belongs to a certain route path.
So for example, if I know that I want
to visit the meals page
and that the meals page depends on data that changed now,
I can tell NextJS to revalidate the /meals path.
And with that, that path would be revalidated.
Now what's important is that,
by default, only that path will be revalidated,
no nested paths.
So if I had some nested path there in my meals folder,
that also depends on all the meals data,
I would have to revalidate that separately.
Alternatively, you can pass a second argument
to revalidate path and set this to layout.
The default is page, which means that simply this one page
for this one path will be revalidated.
If you set it to layout,
it's the layout that will be revalidated,
which as you learned, also wraps nested pages,
and therefore, with this,
all nested pages would be revalidated as well.
And revalidate simply means
that NextJS throws away the cache that is associated
with those pages.
So, for example, the cached pages themselves.
Now here, I don't care about any nested pages
because the dynamic page here isn't pre-generated anyways
in our current setup
and the share page doesn't depend on the meals data.
So I'm fine with just revalidating /meals.
If you would want to revalidate all the pages
of your entire website, you could, by the way, do that
by targeting slash and then setting the mode to layout.
But here, I'm fine with just revalidating the meals path.
Well, and with that done, if we now run npm run build again
to build all those pages again,
they will still be pre-generated and cached,
but now that cache should be revalidated
and partially cleared once we added a new meal.
So if I now run npm start again
to start that development server,
and I then add another new meal,
like this, picking the same image as always,
if I submit that,
it takes a bit longer here, which is a good sign
because it's taking longer
because it loaded all those meals again.
And here we are, now the image is missing,
we'll take care of that in just a second.
But the meal is there and that's of course a good sign.
In addition, we got these Fetching meals logs back here,
which also proves that this is now working as intended.

lectures.title: Don't Store Files Locally On The Filesystem!

cues.en: So now that we understood how caching worked
and we fixed that problem related to it,
let's focus on that missing image.
Why was that image missing
when we added a new meal
whilst running this production server?
Well, the image was missing
because we store those images in this public folder
and they're in the images folder.
The problem with this approach just is that this folder
is available during development,
but for production,
it's actually copied into this .next folder
and it's this .next folder,
which also contains all those cached pages
and so on, hat will be used
by the running NextJS production server.
If you then thereafter add new images
into the public folder, those will be ignored
because the production server doesn't care.
So when you deploy your next project,
you therefore technically don't even have
to deploy the public folder.
NextJS is not interested in it.
Now, that's, of course, a problem for our app here
because we do store images in that public folder.
Well, this behavior is described
in the official NextJS documentation
and there they therefore recommend
that you should store any files that are generated
at run time, essentially, using extra file storage services
like AWS S3.
Now, since working with a provider like S3
is now really a bit beyond the scope
of this course, we'll ignore this problem here.
However, after this lecture, in the next lecture,
you'll find a text lecture where I do describe
how you could use AWS S3
for storing and serving your user-generated images.
You don't have to implement that.
You can ignore it for this demo,
but if you're interested in learning how that would work,
that next lecture is for you.
All that, we are now finally pretty much done
with this application here.
Now I will quickly fix a styling error,
which I only just detected, which has been fixed
in the attachments I provided to you though,
so you already got the right styles earlier, but here,
I'll fix it
by moving position relative in the meal-item.module CSS file
from this meal header selector to the image selector.
Again, I did already fix that in the attachments
I provided to you, so you don't have to do anything
and you got the right styles all the time already.
But now here for me, those meals also look a bit better,
but that's just one thing.
The more important last step I want to go through
together with you is the page metadata
that you can add to your pages.
And you can see that in the root layout.JS file,
there we have a metadata constant
that's being exported and that's not some random constant,
but instead, NextJS is looking for exported variables
or constants called metadata
in all your page or layout files.
And then in this metadata object,
you can set some metadata fields,
which is also described in the official documentation.
There, you can find details about all the fields
you can set on this metadata object
and attached you find a link to this documentation
so that you can explore in depth
which fields can be set there.
In short, this metadata constant allows you to add
a bunch of metadata, which is then, for example,
exposed to search engine crawlers
or which shows up when you are sharing a link to a page
on X or Facebook.
Now here, I'll keep it fairly simple,
but I wanna add a title and description to every page.
Now, if you add this metadata to a layout,
it will automatically be added to all the pages
that are wrapped by that layout
unless a page specifies its own metadata.
In that case, the page metadata wins.
Any nested layout metadata would also win
over that root layout metadata,
but by setting this metadata here,
every page will at least have this basic metadata.
But now of course, I wanna set more specific metadata
for sum of my pages.
For example, for that all meals page.
There, it would be nice to have some metadata
and we can therefore add it by simply exporting
this metadata constant there as well.
And then here we could set the title to all meals,
and then maybe add a description of
browse the delicious meals shared
by our vibrant community, something like this.
If you do that and you go to that meals page, you'll see
that if you reload, you have this all meals title here.
And if you take a look at the page source,
you will also find this description meta tag in there,
which contains your description text as content.
Here it is.
So that's how you can add metadata,
but how can you add metadata to dynamic pages
where the title and the description
depends on the concrete data that has been loaded?
Adding static metadata like this
typically doesn't do the trick there.
For dynamic pages, you can add metadata
by not exporting a constant or variable named metadata,
but by instead exporting an async function called
generateMetadata.
And it must be called like this
because NextJS is also looking for functions like this.
If it doesn't find any other metadata,
it's checking whether there is such a function,
and if there is such a function, NextJS will execute it
for you and then it's your job
to return such a metadata object in that function.
Now how does that help us with dynamic data?
Well, this function receives the same data
our page component receives as props.
So here we also get an object with a params key,
and that of course allows us to get the meal
for which the metadata should be generated
by simply accessing mealSlug and passing that to getMeal.
Well, and with that, we can then return a title
that's set equal to meal title
and a description that's set to meal.summary,
for example, and that's
how we can generate the metadata for a dynamic page.
With that, if we now visit a meal, we can see its title,
its name represented here in the tab title.
Now if we enter some invalid slug here,
we now get an error though instead of the not found page
because the metadata is actually generated first
and this now simply fails.
When I try to access title on meal,
that fails because meal is undefined.
So therefore we should actually add this if check here,
where we check whether the meal is maybe not defined,
and called the notFound function if it isn't,
inside of generate metadata to ensure
that we show the notFound page if generating
the metadata fails, which it does
if we don't find that meal.
With that, you see that now we get
that meal not found page again,
but that's how we can handle that metadata.
And that's now it for this section.
In this section, we had a in-depth look into NextJS
using this App Router
and you learned how you can set up routes
by using the file system instead of app
and by using these special file names
like page.js and layout.js.
You also learned about other special files
like error.js for handling errors,
or not-found.js for handling not found errors,
or the loading js file, which I'm not using here,
but which we used temporarily
to show some loading state on the screen.
Though you learned that you have more granular control
by using suspense, which is what we then did.
Now you also learned how to configure dynamic routes
where some path segments aren't known in advance,
like here, where we load pages for individual meals,
where we don't know in advance how many meals we'll have
and most importantly, you learned that all those pages
in the end just export standard React components,
but that those components
are kind of special when using NextJS.
That they are server components
that are executed on the server,
that are rendered on the server, therefore.
And it's not just those page components,
but instead all components
unless you explicitly opt out of this behavior
by adding this use client directive to convert a file
and its components into a client component,
which then is rendered on the client and which then
therefore may use client side functionality like useState
or handling user events.
You therefore also learned that you can take advantage
of those Server components by fetching data directly
inside of those components.
There is no need to use user effect
and send requests to separate backends.
Instead, you can fetch the data from right
inside your Server components.
And you can just fetch the data,
you also learned about Server Actions, async functions
that either have to use Server directive inside of them
or that are stored in a file with used Server at the top.
And the special thing about those Server Actions is
that you can assign them as values to the action prop
on form elements, either directly
or as we're doing it here with help of useFormState,
which is a hook provided by react-dom
to handle responses returned by the Server action function
and then potentially update the UI based on those responses.
Like here where we are conditionally
showing an error message.
Speaking of updating the UI based on Server Actions,
you also learned about the useFormStatus hook,
which can be used to find out whether a form
is currently being submitted
or not, which can then be used to update the UI accordingly.
Now, related to all of that, you also learned
that NextJS does some pretty aggressive caching
and that therefore you should call revalidatePath
whenever you change some data to make sure
that the latest data is fetched
and represented on your pages.
And you also saw that it can be dangerous
if you never test your app in production mode
because everything worked in development mode
in our app here,
but then suddenly the data was missing in production mode.
So this is an important function
and an important concept to understand in general.
Now, last but not least, we also talked about metadata
that can be added to pages, static metadata
as we have it here or dynamically generated metadata.
And therefore at this point you
have a super solid NextJS foundation
and you are ready to use NextJS
with its App Router in your future projects.
